title: Hare Krishna

cards: A group walks down a city street, in London or New York or Sydney, in saffron and white, with a drum and small hand cymbals, singing. Hare Krishna, Hare Krishna. People stare, or smile, or cross the street.
It can look like something new. It isn't. That same song filled the streets of a town in Bengal in the fifteen-hundreds, sung by a man who, his followers say, danced until he fell to the ground.
And the words themselves are older still.

teach.b: Here are the words. Hare Krishna, Hare Krishna, Krishna Krishna, Hare Hare. Hare Rama, Hare Rama, Rama Rama, Hare Hare.
Sixteen words, only three names. Krishna, the one you followed from the prison at midnight to the chariot. Rama, the prince who came home to a city of lamps.

And Hare, which many devotees understand as calling on Hara, Radha, the love and energy of God, and which others hear as a form of Hari, Vishnu, the one who takes away. That's the maha-mantra, the great mantra.
It appears, with the Rama half first, in a short text called the Kali-Santarana Upanishad, which says that in this age, the simplest way across is the name.

teach.h: CHAITANYA TAKES IT TO THE STREET.
teach.b: Then, in the early fifteen-hundreds, in Navadvip in Bengal, came Chaitanya Mahaprabhu. His followers remember him as Krishna himself, come as a devotee, taking the names out of quiet rooms and into the street.
Singing together, with drums and cymbals, is called sankirtan, and Chaitanya made it the heart of the practice. Why out loud?

teach.h: THE NAME IS KRISHNA, IN SOUND.
teach.b: Here's the teaching: in Chaitanya's tradition, the holy name isn't just a word about Krishna. It is not different from Krishna himself, present in sound.
So singing it together is the practice for this age, and sung, it reaches everyone in earshot, even the ones crossing the street. In 1965, a monk in his line, an elderly man named A. C.
Bhaktivedanta Swami, arrived in New York with almost nothing. Before long he was singing it in a city park. That's where the group you saw comes from.

how: Gaudiya Vaishnavas, including members of ISKCON, chant the Hare Krishna maha-mantra daily on beads, often sixteen rounds of 108, and sing it together in kirtan with drums and cymbals, at home, in temples and in the street.

games.why: he takes it into the street. sankirtan, singing together with drums and cymbals, becomes the heart of the practice.

practice: This one isn't whispered: if you're somewhere you can, sing it softly, to any simple tune or on one note. Hare Krishna, Hare Krishna, Krishna Krishna, Hare Hare. Hare Rama, Hare Rama, Rama Rama, Hare Hare.

Once through is one round; keep going, and tap your knee for a drum if you like. If you don't pray, let it simply be singing, and notice what singing does that speaking doesn't; if you can't make noise, mouth the words.

wordCard.voice: Hare Krishna. The maha-mantra: sixteen words, three names, meant to be sung out loud.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Hare, calling on Hara (Radha) or Hari, and Krishna, the dark one, the all-attractive.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: sankirtan, God's name, sung together. In this tradition, the name is Krishna himself, in sound. See you tomorrow.
